nutshell: Transferable black-box adversarial attacks on person re-ID need to fool unseen models and datasets, but prior vision-language-model-guided attacks only disrupt holistic image or text embeddings, under-attacking fine-grained pedestrian attributes. AP-Attack instead learns per-attribute textual-inversion networks that map a pedestrian image to five attribute-specific pseudo-word tokens (top clothing, bottom clothing, hairstyle, shoes, bag) plugged into one fixed prompt template, then attacks by pushing each attribute's adversarial token away from its benign counterpart and toward the least-similar negative token, achieving more thorough attribute-level disruption and better cross-model/cross-dataset transferability.
contributions: Attribute-aware textual inversion: five lightweight 3-layer fully-connected networks map a frozen CLIP visual embedding to five attribute-specific pseudo-tokens, which are composed into one fixed template sentence ('A photo of a person wearing S1 on top, S2 underneath, S3 hairstyle, S4 shoes, carrying S5') and trained with an ID-aware contrastive loss so the tokens are consistent across images of the same identity - the first use of textual inversion for fine-grained, per-attribute (rather than per-instance/global) semantic disruption in transferable adversarial attacks.

A prompt-driven semantic attack loss applied independently within each of the five attribute semantic spaces (triplet-style: push the adversarial token away from its own benign token, pull it toward the batch's least-similar negative token), combined with a standard surrogate-model feature attack loss to jointly optimize the adversarial generator.

New state-of-the-art transferability across cross-dataset, cross-model, and the hardest cross-model&dataset settings (Tables 1-3), most notably +22.9% mean Drop Rate over the prior best prompt-driven method (PDCL-Attack) in the cross-model&dataset setting, plus consistent gains against three defenses (adversarial training, JPEG compression, randomization; Table 4) and against three structurally different re-id paradigms - self-supervised PASS, auxiliary-feature PGFA, and CLIP-based CLIP-ReID (Table 6).
deficiencies: The paper's own ablation (Table 5) shows the fine-grained attribute decomposition - the headline contribution - contributes a modest final step: adding any CLIP text-embedding loss at all takes mDR from 40.3% to 66.2%, and the fine-grained attribute design only adds a further +6.2 points (to 72.4%). Most of the overall improvement over the pure-image-feature baseline comes from using CLIP text embeddings at all, not specifically from the per-attribute fine-graining that is marketed as the core idea.

The five attributes (top, bottom, hairstyle, shoes, bag) are fixed by a hand-written English template with no discussion of what happens when an attribute is absent or occluded (e.g. no bag, unclear hairstyle), and no ablation varying the attribute set or count to show the design is not arbitrary.

The interpretability check for the inversion networks (Fig. 3 word-cloud) is a soft, subjective sanity check: a ChatGPT-generated attribute vocabulary is nearest-neighbor-matched to the learned pseudo-tokens by cosine similarity, which shows the tokens correlate with plausible words but doesn't quantitatively verify they encode the intended attribute rather than some other correlated visual cue.

All baseline methods in Tables 1-3 are re-trained by the authors themselves for the comparison ('re-trained with surrogate model IDE on DukeMTMC for fair comparisons') rather than using independently-published baseline numbers, so every reported gap depends entirely on the authors' own reimplementation quality with no external cross-check available.
notable: The reference list contains two separate duplicate-citation errors: [54] and [55] are the exact same paper (Yang et al., 'Prompt-driven contrastive learning for transferable adversarial attacks,' ECCV) cited twice under different years (2024 and 2025), and independently [62] and [63] are also the same paper (Zhang et al., 'Beyond ImageNet Attack') cited twice under different years (2021 and 2022). This is the same duplicate-citation bibliography pattern seen repeatedly elsewhere in this literature batch (e.g. the BMVC2023 SANet paper, BMDG, EgoPoints) - two independent instances in one paper's bibliography makes it look like a systematic reference-manager/LaTeX artifact rather than an isolated slip.
